Ahaz
AY-haz
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped" or "possessor"; a shortened form of Yehoachaz, "Yahweh has grasped" (which is the form preserved in 2 Chronicles 28 in some manuscripts). The same root produced the Assyrian-tablet name Yauhazi (the form by which Tiglath-Pileser III recorded him in his royal annals).

📖 Biblical Definition

Ahaz (c. 735 — 715 BC) was the twelfth king of Judah (2 Kings 16; 2 Chronicles 28; Isaiah 7), son of the faithful Jotham, whose sixteen-year reign produced the deepest apostasy in pre-exilic Judahite history before Manasseh and whose famous interview with the prophet Isaiah produced the most theologically loaded sign-prophecy in the Old Testament (Isa 7:14, the Immanuel prophecy). Ahaz reigned during the great Syro-Ephraimite crisis (c. 734-732 BC), when Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel allied to depose him and replace him with a puppet ("the son of Tabeel," Isa 7:6), planning to detach Judah from any Assyrian-loyalty axis. Isaiah confronted him at the conduit of the upper pool with a two-fold word: do not fear these two smoking firebrands (Isa 7:4) and ask the LORD for any sign in heaven or earth to confirm the promise (Isa 7:10-12). Ahaz famously refused the sign with sham-piety: "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD." Isaiah then gave the sign anyway: "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isa 7:14) — the prophecy Matthew 1:23 applies to the virgin birth of Christ. Ahaz refused the sign and made his own political solution: he stripped the temple and palace treasuries to bribe Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria to attack Damascus and Israel for him (2 Kings 16:7-9). Tiglath-Pileser obliged but extracted from Ahaz a vassal-treaty that put Judah under permanent Assyrian tribute. Ahaz further apostatized: he saw an altar at Damascus he admired, sent its measurements home to the priest Urijah, who built a copy in the Jerusalem temple before Ahaz returned; Ahaz then offered on the new altar and moved the bronze altar of Yahweh aside (2 Kings 16:10-16). He shut up the doors of the temple of the LORD entirely toward the end of his reign (2 Chr 28:24), built high places "in every several city of Judah," and burned his own sons in the fire to Molech in the Valley of Hinnom (2 Chr 28:3).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Twelfth king of Judah (c. 735-715 BC); son of the faithful Jotham; the Immanuel-prophecy recipient (Isa 7:14) who refused the sign offered by Isaiah; bribed Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria; built a Damascene altar in the temple; burned his own sons to Molech; shut the temple doors.

AHAZ, proper noun. Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped" (shortened from Yehoachaz, "Yahweh has grasped").

Twelfth king of Judah (c. 735-715 BC); son of Jotham; father of Hezekiah.

Reigned during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (c. 734-732 BC); recipient of Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy (Isa 7:14) which he refused as a sign.

Bribed Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria to attack Damascus and Israel (2 Kings 16:7-9); built a Damascene-pattern altar in the Jerusalem temple; sacrificed his own sons in the fire to Molech (2 Chr 28:3); shut the doors of the temple (2 Chr 28:24).

Appears in Assyrian royal annals as Yauhazi.

📖 Key Scripture

Isaiah 7:9 — "If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established."

Isaiah 7:14 — "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

2 Chronicles 28:3 — "Moreover [Ahaz] burnt incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and burnt his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen whom the LORD had cast out before the children of Israel."

2 Kings 16:7-8 — "So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son... And Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD, and in the treasures of the king's house, and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Ahaz is corrupted when his refusal of Isaiah's sign is read as humble piety rather than as the deliberate evasion Isaiah immediately condemned, when the Immanuel prophecy is detached from the historical setting that gave it weight, or when his vassalage to Tiglath-Pileser is excused as political necessity rather than read as the covenant-betrayal Scripture intends.

expand to see more

Sham-piety refusal misread. "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD" sounds reverent until one reads the next verse: "And [Isaiah] said, Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign" (Isa 7:13-14). Isaiah saw through it instantly: this was not piety, it was unbelief dressed up in pious-sounding refusal because Ahaz had already decided to bribe Tiglath-Pileser and did not want a Yahweh-sign that would have committed him to trust the LORD instead. The reader should hear Isaiah's pastoral exasperation in 7:13.

Political-necessity excuse. Modern readings sometimes treat Ahaz's appeal to Assyria as understandable real-politik: faced with the Syro-Ephraimite alliance threatening to depose him, what choice did he have but to call on the only superpower available? The text rejects this defense. Isaiah explicitly offered him an alternative: trust the LORD's word about the Syro-Ephraimite threat (Isa 7:4-9). Ahaz refused not because no alternative existed but because trust-in-Yahweh was the alternative he refused. The wages of his refusal: a hundred years of Assyrian vassalage, the eventual fall of Israel (722 BC), and the near-fall of Judah (Sennacherib at the gates in 701).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped," from achaz ("to grasp, take hold"). Shortened from Yehoachaz, "Yahweh has grasped." Twelfth king of Judah (c. 735-715 BC).

Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped, possessor"; from achaz ("to grasp, take hold")

Shortened form of Yehoachaz — "Yahweh has grasped"; the longer form appears in Assyrian sources as Yauhazi

Twelfth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 735-715 BC)

Son of Jotham; father of Hezekiah

Recipient of Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy at the upper-pool conduit (Isa 7:1-25); the New Testament cites Isa 7:14 of the virgin birth (Matt 1:23)

Usage

"Ahaz — the apostate twelfth king of Judah who refused Isaiah's offered sign."

"If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established (Isa 7:9) — the prophetic warning he ignored."

"Father of Hezekiah; the deepest apostate before Manasseh; the king to whom the Immanuel prophecy was first delivered."
